title: Personal Pronouns and PNG Agreement
subtitle: Matching subjects to verbal Person-Number-Gender suffixes
keyPoint: Finite verbs in Telugu must conjugate with suffixes that reflect the person, number, and gender of the subject pronoun.

mistakes.note: First person subject (నేను) must end with -ను, not the masculine third person -డు.
Feminine third person singular subjects (ఆమె) pair with -ది, not masculine -డు.
Second person singular (నువ్వు) requires the agreement suffix -వు.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'నేను పాలు ___.' (I will drink milk)
quiz.explanation: The first-person singular pronoun 'నేను' requires the verbal suffix '-ను'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'అతను నడుస్తూ ___.' (He will go walking)
quiz.explanation: 'అతను' (he) is third-person masculine singular, requiring '-డు'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'నువ్వు పుస్తకం ___.' (You will read a book)
quiz.explanation: 'నువ్వు' takes the second-person singular informal ending '-వు'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'ఆమె రేపు మా ఇంటికి ___.' (She will come to our house tomorrow)
quiz.explanation: Third-person singular non-masculine (she/it) takes '-ది' (changing here to 'వస్తుంది').

tip: Notice how the pronoun's final syllable often echoes the verb's ending: నే-ను ends in -ను, నువ్-వు ends in -వు, and మే-ము ends in -ము!

title: Oblique Noun Stems and Core Postpositions
subtitle: Inflecting nouns before attaching locative, instrumental, and dative suffixes
keyPoint: Telugu postpositions attach directly to the oblique stem of nouns, which frequently alters endings like -ము to -ం- or changes final vowels.

examples.en: వారి ఊరిలో ఒక పెద్ద చెరువు ఉంది.

mistakes.note: The irregular noun 'ఇల్లు' must mutate to its oblique form 'ఇంటి' before attaching postpositions.
'చేయి' (hand) changes to the oblique form 'చేతి' before case suffixes like -లో.
Nouns ending in -రు often alter their final vowel to -రి- before postpositions.

quiz.question: Attach the locative suffix '-లో' (in) to 'ఇల్లు' (house): 'ఆమె ___ ఉంది.'
quiz.explanation: The oblique stem of 'ఇల్లు' is 'ఇంటి-', making 'ఇంటిలో' (or 'ఇంట్లో').

quiz.question: Choose the correct dative form for 'రాముడు': 'ఈ పుస్తకం ___ ఇవ్వండి.'
quiz.explanation: Masculine nouns in -డు change to oblique -డి before dative -కి.

quiz.question: Attach '-తో' (with) to 'కలం' (pen): 'నేను ___ సంతకం చేశాను.'
quiz.explanation: The postposition '-తో' attaches directly to the stem 'కలం' giving 'కలంతో'.

quiz.question: Attach '-లో' (in) to 'ఊరు' (village): 'మా ___ అందమైన తోటలు ఉన్నాయి.'
quiz.explanation: The oblique stem of 'ఊరు' is 'ఊరి-', yielding 'ఊరిలో'.

tip: Pay special attention to nouns ending in -లు or -డు: 'పాలు' becomes 'పాల-', 'కాలు' becomes 'కాలి-', and words ending in -ము turn cleanly into -ం-!

title: Zero-Copula Equational Sentences vs Undu (Existence)
subtitle: Contrasting identity (A = B) with presence/location using 'ఉండు'
keyPoint: Telugu states identity or character by placing two noun phrases together without any verb, but uses the verb 'ఉండు' to express existence or location.

mistakes.note: Do not insert 'ఉన్నాడు' to mean 'is' when stating someone's profession or identity; Telugu uses zero copula.
Use 'లేదు' (not 'కాదు') when negating presence or location.
Use 'కాదు' when negating identity or ownership ('This is not my house').

quiz.question: Choose the correct phrase for 'Suresh is a teacher': 'సురేష్ ___.'
quiz.explanation: Identity statements require no copular verb, simply juxtaposition of subject and predicate noun.

quiz.question: Complete the locational sentence: 'పిల్లి కుర్చీ కింద ___.' (The cat is under the chair)
quiz.explanation: Non-human singular subjects located somewhere require the third-person neuter existential verb 'ఉంది'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'This is not water'?
quiz.explanation: Negating the identity of a thing ('X is not Y') uses 'కాదు'.

quiz.question: Complete: 'రాజు తరగతిలో ___.' (Raju is not in class)
quiz.explanation: Negating location/presence for a third-person masculine singular subject uses 'లేడు'.

tip: Remember: 'కాదు' denies WHAT something is, while 'లేదు / లేడు / లేరు' denies WHERE something is or IF it exists!

title: Dative Subject Constructions with Kavali and Telusu
subtitle: Expressing needs, desires, and knowledge where the experiencer takes -కి/-కు
keyPoint: In Telugu, feelings, needs (కావాలి), and states of knowing (తెలుసు) treat the experiencer as an indirect dative target marked with -కి or -కు.

mistakes.note: The experiencer of 'కావాలి' must take the dative suffix (నాకు), not the nominative pronoun (నేను).
Knowledge predicates like 'తెలుసు' require the dative pronoun 'నీకు', never nominative 'నువ్వు'.
The negative of 'కావాలి' is 'వద్దు' (or 'అక్కర్లేదు'), not 'కావద్దు'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: '___ ఆకలిగా ఉంది, అన్నం కావాలి.' (I am hungry, I want food)
quiz.explanation: 'కావాలి' requires the dative case pronoun 'నాకు' (to me).

quiz.question: Choose the correct translation for 'Do you know?': '___ తెలుసా?'
quiz.explanation: The experiential verb 'తెలుసు' pairs with the dative form 'నీకు'.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I do not want tea'?
quiz.explanation: 'వద్దు' is the standard negative equivalent to 'కావాలి' when rejecting an item.

quiz.question: Complete: 'రమేష్___ ఈ విషయం తెలియదు.' (Ramesh does not know this matter)
quiz.explanation: Proper names ending in consonants or regular vowels take the dative '-కి' (రమేష్‌కి).

tip: English says 'I want X' or 'I know X', but Telugu thinks 'To me, X is desirable' (నాకు X కావాలి) or 'To me, X is known' (నాకు X తెలుసు)!

title: Present Continuous Tense with -tunna-
subtitle: Forming ongoing actions using the durative infix and PNG markers
keyPoint: The present continuous tense is formed by joining the verb stem to the durative marker -తున్న- (-tunna-) followed by personal agreement endings.

mistakes.note: With 'నేను', the continuous suffix must terminate in first-person '-ను', not non-masculine '-ది'.
Third-person masculine singular 'అతను' requires the ending '-డు'.
Plural subject 'వాళ్ళు' demands the plural personal marker '-రు'.

quiz.question: Complete the ongoing action: 'నేను పాట ___.' (I am listening to a song)
quiz.explanation: 'నేను' requires the first-person singular continuous form 'వింటున్నాను'.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'నువ్వు ఎక్కడికి ___?' (Where are you going?)
quiz.explanation: 'నువ్వు' takes the second-person singular ending '-వు', giving 'వెళ్తున్నావు'.

quiz.question: Complete: 'వాళ్ళు బంతి ఆట ___.' (They are playing ball)
quiz.explanation: Plural human pronoun 'వాళ్ళు' pairs with the suffix '-రు' ('ఆడుతున్నారు').

quiz.question: Complete: 'ఆమె ఉత్తరం ___.' (She is writing a letter)
quiz.explanation: Third-person feminine singular pronoun 'ఆమె' agrees with '-ది' ('రాస్తున్నది' / 'రాస్తోంది').

tip: In everyday spoken Telugu, the feminine/neuter continuous '-తున్నది' (-tunnadi) is almost universally contracted to '-తోంది' (-tondi), as in 'చేస్తోంది' or 'వెళ్తోంది'!

title: Imperative Forms: Informal vs Polite
subtitle: Giving commands, invitations, and requests politely and informally
keyPoint: Add -u or use the basic stem for casual imperatives with peers, but attach the honorific suffix -aṇḍi (-అండి) to show respect or address elders.

mistakes.note: When using the formal pronoun మీరు (meeru), always pair it with the polite imperative ending -aṇḍi (-ండి/-రండి).
The casual pronoun నువ్వు (nuvvu) requires the informal imperative form, not the honorific -aṇḍi.
Use 'రండి' (come in) rather than 'పోండి' (go away/get lost) when welcoming guests inside.

quiz.question: Please speak politely to an elder: 'Please speak!'
quiz.explanation: The polite imperative suffix is -ండి (-aṇḍi), yielding మాట్లాడండి.

quiz.question: Tell your younger brother casually: 'Eat!'
quiz.explanation: The informal singular imperative of 'to eat' is simply తిను (tinu).

quiz.question: Irregular imperative: Address a respected visitor and say 'Please come!'
quiz.explanation: The irregular polite imperative of 'to come' (వచ్చు) is రండి (raṇḍi).

quiz.question: Complete the informal instruction: 'నువ్వు ఉత్తరం ___.' (Write!)
quiz.explanation: The informal imperative for 'to write' addressed to నువ్వు is రాయి (raayi) or రాయు (raayu).

tip: Attach -aṇḍi to practically any casual verb stem to instantly turn it into a warm, polite invitation!

title: Past Tense Stem Classes and Mutations
subtitle: Forming the past tense with the marker -ina- and stem alternations
keyPoint: The Telugu past tense is formed by appending the past marker -ina- (or its colloquial mutated variant -æ-) to the verb stem before personal gender-number agreement suffixes.

mistakes.note: చూస్తాను is future/habitual; completed past actions require past inflection like చూశాను.
Verbs agree with subject gender: ఆమె (she) takes -indi, whereas -aaḍu is reserved for masculine subjects.
First-person plural మేము requires the agreement ending -aamu, not singular -aanu.

quiz.question: Choose the correct past form: 'నిన్న ఆమె బాగా ___.' (She sang well)
quiz.explanation: The feminine 3rd person singular past agreement ending is -indi (పాడింది).

quiz.question: Choose the correct past form: 'మేము బడికి ___.' (We went to school)
quiz.explanation: The 1st person plural past suffix is -aamu (వెళ్లాము).

quiz.question: Choose the correct past form: 'అతను నిన్న ఉత్తరం ___.' (He wrote a letter)
quiz.explanation: The masculine 3rd person singular past suffix is -aaḍu (రాశాడు).

quiz.question: Choose the correct past form: 'వారు నిన్న ___.' (They came yesterday)
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person epicene plural marker is -aaru (వచ్చారు).

tip: In everyday spoken Telugu, the formal past cluster -in- fuses with personal endings into long vowels: చేశాను (I did) instead of చేసినాను.

title: Future-Habitual Tense with -taa-
subtitle: Expressing recurring daily routines and forthcoming future plans
keyPoint: The infix -taa- / -tuu- attaches directly to the verb base to indicate both regular everyday habits and events scheduled to happen in the future.

mistakes.note: వెళ్లాను is past tense; an event planned for tomorrow (రేపు) requires the future marker -taa- (వెళ్తాను).
The pronoun ఆమె (she) takes the feminine future suffix -tundi, while -taaḍu is masculine.
Third person plural వాళ్లు (they) requires the agreement ending -aaru (వస్తారు).

quiz.question: Fill the routine action: 'నేను ప్రతిరోజూ ఉదయం ___.' (I read)
quiz.explanation: The 1st person singular future-habitual form is చదువుతాను.

quiz.question: Fill the future action: 'రవి రేపు క్రికెట్ ___.' (Ravi will play)
quiz.explanation: Ravi is 3rd person masculine singular, taking the ending -taaḍu (ఆడతాడు).

quiz.question: Express a habitual truth: 'ఆవు పాలు ___.' (The cow gives milk)
quiz.explanation: Animals and non-human singular nouns take the 3rd person non-masculine suffix -tundi (ఇస్తుంది).

quiz.question: Complete the polite question: 'మీరు రేపు మా ఆఫీసుకు ___?' (Will you come?)
quiz.explanation: Formal second person మీరు pairs with the polite interrogative -taaraa (వస్తారా).

tip: Telugu does not have distinct grammatical forms for 'I am going tomorrow' versus 'I go every day'; both use this single future-habitual form!

title: Distinct Negators: Ledu, Kaadu, and Vaddu
subtitle: Navigating absence, identity negation, and negative desires
keyPoint: Use లేదు (ledu) for non-existence or past negation, కాదు (kaadu) for denying identity or qualities, and వద్దు (vaddu) for prohibition or rejecting an offer.

cells: It is not (X is not Y)

mistakes.note: To negate identities or professions (He is not a teacher), use కాదు, not లేదు.
'నాకు టీ లేదు' means 'I do not have tea'. To say 'I do not want tea', use వద్దు.
For completed past events ('did not see'), suffix the infinitive with లేదు, not వద్దు.

quiz.question: Deny possession or presence: 'గదిలో ఎవరూ ___.' (There is no one in the room)
quiz.explanation: Absence or non-existence is expressed using లేదు (ledu).

quiz.question: Deny identity: 'ఇది మా ఊరు ___.' (This is not our village)
quiz.explanation: Negating equivalence or identity ('X is not Y') requires కాదు (kaadu).

quiz.question: Politely decline an offer: 'నాకు మిఠాయి ___.' (I don't want sweets)
quiz.explanation: Rejecting or refusing an object ('do not want') requires వద్దు (vaddu).

quiz.question: Negate a past action: 'మేము నిన్న మార్కెట్‌కు ___.' (We did not go)
quiz.explanation: Past action negation is formed by adding లేదు to the infinitive (వెళ్లలేదు).

tip: Remember: లేదు = 'is not there / did not'; కాదు = 'is not that thing'; వద్దు = 'do not want / do not do!'

title: Past Participle (Converb) in -i for Chaining Actions
subtitle: Connecting sequential temporal clauses smoothly with -i
keyPoint: Form the Telugu verbal participle by adding -i to the verbal root, allowing you to string together consecutive actions before concluding with a final conjugated verb.

cells: Having watched the movie, we left

mistakes.note: Native Telugu rarely connects chronological actions with and (మరియు); chain them using the converb -i (తిని) instead.
Do not repeat the subject pronoun when clauses share the same subject in a converbial chain.
Use the valid converb ending -i (చూసి), never the bare raw root.

quiz.question: Chain the sequence: 'అతను కాఫీ ___ ఆఫీసుకు వెళ్లాడు.' (Having drunk coffee, he went to office)
quiz.explanation: The past participle (converb) of తాగు is తాగి (taagi).

quiz.question: Combine consecutive verbs: 'ఆమె ఉత్తరం ___ పోస్ట్ చేసింది.' (Having written the letter, she posted it)
quiz.explanation: The converb of రాయు is రాసి (raasi).

quiz.question: Select the correct chained converb: 'పిల్లలు పాఠం ___ పరీక్ష రాశారు.' (Having learned the lesson, the kids took the exam)
quiz.explanation: The converbial participle of నేర్చుకొను is నేర్చుకుని (having learned).

quiz.question: Fill the linked clause: 'మిత్రులు ఇంటికి ___ భోజనం చేశారు.' (The friends, having come home, ate dinner)
quiz.explanation: The past participle converb of వచ్చు is వచ్చి (vacci).

tip: You can chain multiple -i converbs consecutively in a single sentence (e.g., లేచి, స్నానం చేసి, తిని వెళ్లాడు) — only the very last verb takes tense and personal endings!

title: Question Clitic -aa vs Doubt Clitic -o
subtitle: Forming yes/no polar questions and expressing uncertainty
keyPoint: Attach the clitic -aa to the focus word or verb to form a yes/no question, and attach -o to express doubt, indefiniteness, or indirect questions.

useCases.label: Expressing Doubt or Wonder
useCases.example: ఆయన రేపు వస్తాడో రాడో నాకు తెలియదు.

mistakes.note: Telugu requires the interrogative suffix -aa on the verb; question intonation alone is unnatural in standard speech.
Use -o on interrogative pronouns to mean 'someone' (indefinite); using -aa turns it into a rhetorical or echo question.
Embedded indirect questions meaning 'whether... or' take the dubitative marker -o, not the direct question marker -aa.

quiz.question: Complete the polar question: 'Are you drinking tea?' -> 'నువ్వు టీ ___?'
quiz.explanation: The polar interrogative marker -aa replaces or lengthens the final vowel of the finite verb (తాగుతావు + ఆ = తాగుతావా).

quiz.question: Choose the form expressing uncertainty: 'I don't know whether he will come' -> 'ఆయన ___ నాకు తెలియదు.'
quiz.explanation: Indirect embedded questions and doubt require the dubitative suffix -o (వస్తాడు + ఓ = వస్తాడో).

quiz.question: Identify the indefinite pronoun meaning 'somewhere':
quiz.explanation: Attaching -o to question words forms indefinites: ఎక్కడ (where) + ఓ = ఎక్కడో (somewhere).

quiz.question: Select the correct sentence for: 'Is this your car?'
quiz.explanation: The noun కారు takes the vowel-lengthened interrogative suffix -aa to ask 'is it a car?'.

tip: To target a specific detail in a sentence, shift -aa from the verb to that specific word: 'నిన్నా వచ్చావు?' means 'Was it yesterday that you came?'

title: Accusative Marker -nu / -ni
subtitle: Differential object marking for animate and definite direct objects
keyPoint: The accusative suffixes -nu (after back vowels u, o) and -ni (after front vowels i, e) are applied to animate beings and definite specific inanimate objects.

mistakes.note: Animate objects (humans and animals) require the accusative marker -ni/-nu; omitting it sounds incomplete.
General non-specific inanimate direct objects (like water or rice) drop the accusative suffix.
The pronoun 'I' (నేను) takes the suppletive accusative stem 'నన్ను' (me), not the genitive stem 'నా'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct object form: 'The teacher praised the student (విద్యార్థి).' -> 'ఉపాధ్యాయుడు ___ మెచ్చుకున్నారు.'
quiz.explanation: Animate nouns ending in -i take -ni in the accusative case (విద్యార్థి + ని = విద్యార్థిని).

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly drops the accusative marker for a non-specific inanimate object?
quiz.explanation: Everyday non-specific mass nouns like 'అన్నం' do not take the accusative marker in ordinary transitive sentences.

quiz.question: Identify the accusative form of 'you' (singular informal):
quiz.explanation: The accusative form of నువ్వు is నిన్ను.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank with the definite object: 'Give me that pen.' -> 'ఆ ___ నాకు ఇవ్వు.'
quiz.explanation: Specific definite inanimate nouns marked with a demonstrative (ఆ) take the accusative marker (కలం + ని = కలాన్ని).

tip: Vowel harmony rule: If the preceding syllable ends in 'i' or 'e', use -ni (పిల్లిని, ఆమెని). If it ends in 'u', use -nu (ఆవును, గురువును).

title: Relative Participles Across Tenses
subtitle: Modifying nouns directly with adjectival verb forms
keyPoint: Telugu forms relative clauses by turning verbs into adjectival participles (-ina for past, -tunna for present continuous, -e for habitual/future) placed directly before the modified noun.

cells: the bus that goes / will go
the guest who did/does not come

useCases.label: Past Completed Event
useCases.example: నిన్న కొన్న పండ్లు చాలా తీపిగా ఉన్నాయి.

useCases.label: Habitual or Future Action
useCases.example: హైదరాబాద్ వెళ్లే రైలు ఏ ప్లాట్‌ఫారమ్‌కు వస్తుంది?

mistakes.note: Telugu does not use English-style relative pronouns (who/which); instead, convert the verb into a relative participle placed before the noun.
Finite verbs (చదివాను) cannot modify a noun; you must use the relative adjectival participle (చదివిన).

mistakes.wrong: చేయని పనికి జీతం రాదు (using wrong negative: చేయక పని)
mistakes.note: Relative adjectival negation requires the participle suffix -ani (చేయని), not the adverbial verbal participle form -ka.

quiz.question: Select the correct participle: 'The boy who is running is my brother.' -> 'అక్కడ ___ అబ్బాయి మా తమ్ముడు.'
quiz.explanation: The present continuous relative participle suffix is -tunna (పరిగెడుతున్న = who is running).

quiz.question: Choose the past relative participle: 'The movie that we saw yesterday.' -> 'మేము నిన్న ___ సినిమా.'
quiz.explanation: The past relative participle is formed by adding -ina to the verbal base (చూడు -> చూసిన).

quiz.question: Complete the sentence with habitual participle: 'The water we drink must be pure.' -> 'మనం ___ నీరు పరిశుభ్రంగా ఉండాలి.'
quiz.explanation: The habitual/generic relative participle uses the suffix -e (తాగే = that one drinks).

quiz.question: Which word is the negative relative participle meaning 'the train that does not stop'?
quiz.explanation: Negative relative participles are formed with root + ani (ఆగు + అని = ఆగని).

tip: Telugu relative clauses precede the head noun entirely. Unlike English 'the book that I read', Telugu structure is '[I read-which] book' (నేను చదివిన పుస్తకం).

title: Conditional (-te) and Concessive (-ina)
subtitle: Expressing 'if' conditions and 'even if / although' concessions
keyPoint: Add -te to the past verbal stem to state conditions ('if'), and add -ina to state concessions ('even if / although').

cells: If it rains, we will stay home.
Even if it rains, we will go.
Even though he didn't study, he passed.

mistakes.note: A conditional -te clause referring to a pending situation must be followed by a future/habitual or modal main verb, not a past tense.
Irregular verb stems shift before -te: చెప్పు becomes చెబితే (or చెప్పినట్లయితే), not చెప్పితే.
Do not attach కూడా to -te for 'even if'; use the dedicated concessive suffix -ina (పడినా).

quiz.question: Complete the 'if' clause: 'If you study well, you will pass.' -> 'బాగా ___ పరీక్ష పాసవుతావు.'
quiz.explanation: The conditional 'if' marker attached to the verbal root is -te (చదివితే).

quiz.question: Select the form meaning 'even if called':
quiz.explanation: The concessive 'even if' form is built by adding -ina to the stem (పిలిచినా).

quiz.question: Choose the negative condition: 'If you do not eat medicine, health won't improve.' -> 'మందులు ___ ఆరోగ్యం బాగుపడదు.'
quiz.explanation: Negative conditionals use the auxiliary -kapote (వేసుకోకపోతే = if you do not take).

quiz.question: What does 'చెప్పినా వినలేదు' mean?
options: He didn't listen even though I told him.
If I tell him, he won't listen.
Because I didn't tell him, he didn't listen.
While telling, he did not listen.
quiz.explanation: చెప్పినా contains the concessive -ina ('even though told'), indicating counter-expectation.

tip: Distinguish between relative participle -ina (short: వచ్చిన మనిషి 'the man who came') and concessive -ina (lengthened vowel -inaa: వచ్చినా 'even if he comes').

title: Modal Auxiliaries with Verbal Infinitive
subtitle: Expressing ability (-galugu) and permission or possibility (-vaccu)
keyPoint: Form the verbal infinitive by suffixing -an/-a to the verb root, then append auxiliary verbs like galugu (can/ability) or vaccu (may/possibility).

cells: must not do / should not do

mistakes.note: Use galugu for internal capability or learned skill; vaccu expresses permission or external possibility.
When asking for permission, the infinitive + vaccu must end with the question clitic -aa (రావచ్చా?).
To express past inability ('could not'), combine the infinitive with leka-poyindi rather than negating galugu with kaadu.

quiz.question: Choose the correct modal for ability: 'I can swim.' -> 'నేను ఈద___.'
quiz.explanation: Infinitive ఈద + గలను (first-person singular of galugu) denotes personal capability: 'I can swim'.

quiz.question: How do you ask for permission: 'May I sit here?'
quiz.explanation: Permission questions combine the infinitive (కూర్చో-) with vaccu and the question marker -aa (కూర్చోవచ్చా?).

quiz.question: Select the modal expressing strict prohibition: 'One must not speak lies.' -> 'అబద్ధాలు చెప్ప___.'
quiz.explanation: The auxiliary koodadu (కూడదు) attached to the infinitive (చెప్ప) indicates prohibition ('must not').

quiz.question: Complete the sentence to mean 'He could not come': 'అతడు ___.'
quiz.explanation: Past inability is expressed using the negative infinitive auxiliary lekapoyadu (రాలేకపోయాడు).

tip: The verb vaccu inflected as an auxiliary is invariable across genders and numbers: 'ఆమె వెళ్లవచ్చు' (she may go) and 'వాళ్లు వెళ్లవచ్చు' (they may go) both use identical forms.

title: Compound Verbs with Auxiliary Konu
subtitle: Expressing actions done for oneself, reflexivity, and gradual change of state
keyPoint: Appending the auxiliary verb కొను (konu) to an invariant verbal base indicates that an action is performed for one's own benefit, reciprocally, or denotes an internal state transition.

cells: To look at oneself / take care

useCases.label: Internal/Mental State
useCases.example: వారు ఆ విషయం గురించి బాగా ఆలోచించుకున్నారు.

mistakes.note: When the action directly benefits the subject, use the auxiliary కొను rather than simple transitive verbs.
Wearing or putting clothes on oneself requires the reflexive వేసుకొను rather than వేయు.
Do not use కొను when the beneficiary or target of the action is completely external to the subject.

quiz.question: I prepared dinner for myself: నేను రాత్రి భోజనం ___.
quiz.explanation: చేసుకున్నాను indicates a 1st person singular past action done for one's own benefit.

quiz.question: She looked at herself in the mirror: ఆమె అద్దంలో ___.
quiz.explanation: చూసుకుంది is the 3rd person feminine past reflexive form matching ఆమె.

quiz.question: Did you (informal) take the money?: నువ్వు డబ్బులు ___?
quiz.explanation: తీసుకున్నావా is the correct 2nd person singular past interrogative form.

quiz.question: The children sat down quietly: పిల్లలు నిశ్శబ్దంగా ___.
quiz.explanation: కూర్చున్నారు is the 3rd person plural past form derived from కూర్చొను.

tip: In conversational Telugu, the past stem of కొను often becomes -క్కున్- (-kkun-), so కొను + past becomes కొనుక్కున్నాను.

title: Causative Verb Formations with -incu
subtitle: Deriving transitive and causative verbs using the verbal suffix -incu
keyPoint: Suffixing -ించు (-incu) to intransitive or simple transitive verb bases derives causative verbs indicating that the subject causes another entity to perform or undergo the action.

cells: To cause to do / have someone do

examples.en: వారు మాకు తమ కొత్త ఇల్లు చూపించారు.

mistakes.note: Use the causative form తినిపించు (to feed) rather than the simple verb తిను (to eat) when feeding someone.
When getting work done through someone else, use the causative చేయించు instead of చేశాను.
నడుచు is intransitive; making someone walk or leading them requires causative నడిపించు.

quiz.question: Mother fed the child milk: తల్లి పిల్లకు పాలు ___.
quiz.explanation: తాగించింది is the 3rd person feminine causative past form of తాగు (to drink).

quiz.question: The teacher made the students write an essay: ఉపాధ్యాయురాలు విద్యార్థులతో వ్యాసం ___.
quiz.explanation: రాయించింది indicates that the female teacher caused the students to write.

quiz.question: They showed us their farm: వారు మాకు తమ పొలం ___.
quiz.explanation: చూపించారు is the respectful plural past causative form of చూడు (to see).

quiz.question: The driver drove the car carefully: డ్రైవర్ కారును జాగ్రత్తగా ___.
quiz.explanation: నడిపించాడు is the causative masculine form indicating driving or steering.

tip: The intermediary agent who is caused to do the action is almost always marked by the instrumental postposition తో (to / with).

title: Complementizer and Purposive Constructions with Ani
subtitle: Forming reported speech, indirect thoughts, intentions, and causal clauses
keyPoint: The verbal participle అని (ani), originating from the defective verb అను (to say), functions as an indispensable quotative marker, complementizer, and purpose conjunction.

cells: Indicating purpose or intent (in order to)

examples.en: ఆమె నాతో నిజం చెప్పలేదని కోపం వచ్చింది.

mistakes.note: Telugu complement clauses cannot simply juxtapose; the quotative అని must link the subordinate clause to the main verb.
Combining dynamic intent with కోసం redundantly is unnatural; use the hortative + అని construction.
In Telugu, the content clause precedes అని and the main verb follows at the end.

quiz.question: I brought an umbrella thinking it might rain: వర్షం పడుతుంది ___ గొడుగు తెచ్చాను.
quiz.explanation: అని connects the anticipated thought or reason directly to the main action.

quiz.question: He said that he would come tomorrow: అతను రేపు ___ అని చెప్పాడు.
quiz.explanation: వస్తానని incorporates the 1st person future marker bound seamlessly to అని in indirect reported speech.

quiz.question: We went there intending to buy mangoes: మేము మామిడిపండ్లు ___ అక్కడికి వెళ్ళాము.
quiz.explanation: కొందామని combines the hortative కొందాము with the quotative purposive marker అని.

quiz.question: I found out that she is not feeling well: ఆమెకు ఆరోగ్యం బాగాలేదు ___ తెలిసింది.
quiz.explanation: అని acts as the complementizer linking the state clause to the cognitive verb తెలిసింది.

tip: When personal verb endings ending in -ను combine with అని, the vowels coalesce: వస్తాను + అని becomes వస్తానని.

title: Participial Nouns (Headless Relatives)
subtitle: Nominalizing relative participles into agentive and abstract demonstratives
keyPoint: Participial nouns are created by fusing verbal adjectives (relative participles) with third-person pronominal suffixes to express 'the one who does' or 'that which did'.

mistakes.note: Avoid clumsy double modification; merge the participle and demonstrative pronoun into చేసినవాడు.
When turning an entire relative clause into an object noun, suffix -ది directly: చెప్పినది.
Do not affix extra case remnants like -డు onto -వారు; use -వాడు for masculine singular and -వారు for plural.

quiz.question: The one (male) who arrived yesterday is my brother: నిన్న ___ మా తమ్ముడు.
quiz.explanation: వచ్చినవాడు fuses the past participle వచ్చిన with the masculine demonstrative suffix -వాడు.

quiz.question: Those who do not work will not eat: పని ___ వారికి తిండి దొరకదు.
quiz.explanation: చేయని is the negative relative participle required for 'those who do not do'.

quiz.question: What you said is correct: నువ్వు ___ నిజమే.
quiz.explanation: అన్నది nominalizes the action neuter-wise to mean 'the thing that was said'.

quiz.question: All those who came to the meeting listened: సమావేశానికి ___ అందరూ విన్నారు.
quiz.explanation: వచ్చినవారు corresponds to the plural human noun 'those who came'.

tip: Neuter participial nouns ending in -ది (e.g., తిన్నది) can mean either the object ('what was eaten') or the feminine/neuter subject ('she/it that ate') depending on context.

title: Passive and Adversative Constructions with Padu
subtitle: Expressing passive voice and involuntary or adversative experiences
keyPoint: The auxiliary verb పడు (padu) joins with verbal infinitive stems ending in -అ (-a) to form formal passive clauses and denote adverse or involuntary experiences.

examples.en: అతను ఆ సమస్య గురించి తీవ్రంగా ఆందోళనపడ్డాడు.

mistakes.note: Attach పడు directly to the short verbal infinitive stem (చదవ-), never to the verbal noun (చదవడం).
Experiential states like భయపడు are inherently intransitive; do not mix causative -పెట్టు with passive forms.
When using the instrumental agent marker చేత (by), the governing verb must be conjugated in the passive voice with పడు.

quiz.question: The bill was approved in assembly: ఆ బిల్లు శాసనసభలో ___.
quiz.explanation: ఆమోదించబడింది is the correct 3rd person neuter passive past formation.

quiz.question: The boy was scared by the sudden noise: అబ్బాయి హఠాత్తుగా వచ్చిన శబ్దానికి ___.
quiz.explanation: భయపడ్డాడు is the experiential masculine past tense meaning 'he felt scared'.

quiz.question: This letter was written by Rama: ఈ ఉత్తరం రాముడి చేత ___.
quiz.explanation: The passive form రాయబడింది agrees with the neuter singular subject ఉత్తరం (letter).

quiz.question: The villagers faced many troubles during the floods: వరదల సమయంలో గ్రామస్తులు ఎన్నో కష్టాలు ___.
quiz.explanation: పడ్డారు agrees with the plural subject గ్రామస్తులు (villagers) in experiencing hardship.

tip: Spoken Telugu prefers active constructions whenever possible; the formal passive with పడు is primarily encountered in news broadcasts, administrative notices, and formal literature.
